{
  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_001",
  "condition": "modernize",
  "rewritten_text": "She was so caught up in admiring those soft blue eyes, chatting and listening, and coming up with all these plans in between, that the evening flew by at an incredible rate. Before she knew it, the supper table, which always marked the end of these gatherings, was all set and ready, and had been moved to the fireplace. With an enthusiasm that went beyond her usual eagerness to do everything well and with attention to detail, and with the genuine warmth of someone who was thrilled with her own ideas, she took charge of the meal, offering and recommending the minced chicken and scalloped oysters with a persistence that she knew would be appreciated by their guests, given the early hour and their polite reservations.

On occasions like this, poor Mr. Woodhouse's feelings were torn. He loved the tradition of laying out a spread, as it had been the custom in his youth, but his conviction that suppers were unhealthy made him regret seeing any food being served. While his hospitality would have welcomed their visitors to everything, his concern for their well-being made him worry that they would overeat.

All he could wholeheartedly recommend was a small bowl of thin gruel, similar to his own. However, as the ladies were comfortably enjoying the nicer dishes, he might suggest, 'Mrs. Bates, why don't you try one of these eggs? A soft-boiled egg isn't unhealthy. Serle is an expert at boiling eggs, and I wouldn't recommend anyone else's. But don't worry, they're very small, as you can see - one of our small eggs won't hurt you. Miss Bates, let Emma give you a little bit of tart - just a very little bit. We only have apple tarts, and you don't have to worry about unhealthy preserves here. I wouldn't advise the custard, though. Mrs. Goddard, would you like half a glass of wine? Just a small half-glass, mixed with water? I don't think it could disagree with you.'

Emma let her father talk, but she made sure their visitors were well taken care of in a much more satisfying way. That evening, she took particular pleasure in seeing them off happy. Miss Smith was just as happy as Emma had intended. As a prominent figure in Highbury, Miss Woodhouse's introduction had caused Miss Smith both excitement and nerves, but the kind and grateful young girl left with highly gratified feelings, delighted with the friendly way Miss Woodhouse had treated her all evening, and even shaken hands with her before leaving.

Harriet Smith soon became a regular at Hartfield. Emma, being quick and decisive, wasted no time in inviting her, encouraging her to visit often, and as they spent more time together, their mutual satisfaction grew. Emma had initially seen Harriet as a potential walking companion, which was something she had been missing since Mrs. Weston's departure. Her father rarely ventured beyond the shrubbery, where two paths were enough for his daily walks, regardless of the season. Since Mrs. Weston's loss, Emma had been looking for someone to share these walks with, and Harriet seemed like the perfect companion."
}

{
  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_002",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "The list Emma created when she was fourteen, I recall, impressed me with her judgment, and I kept it for some time. I'm sure she could make a good list now, but I've given up expecting her to engage in steady reading. She'll never commit to anything that requires effort and patience, or subordinating her imagination to her understanding. Miss Taylor was unable to motivate her, and I doubt Harriet Smith will have any more success. You could never persuade Emma to read as much as you wanted her to. You know that's true."

"I dare say," Mrs. Weston replied with a smile, "that I thought that way at the time, but since we've been apart, I don't recall Emma ever failing to do something I asked of her."

"There's little point in refreshing such a memory," Mr. Knightley said, feeling a pang, and he fell silent for a moment. "But I, who haven't been blinded by personal feelings, must still observe, listen, and remember. Emma has been spoiled by being the most intelligent member of her family. At ten, she could answer questions that puzzled her seventeen-year-old sister. She's always been quick and confident, while Isabella was slow and uncertain. Since she was twelve, Emma has been in charge of the house and everyone in it. With her mother's passing, she lost the only person who could match her. She inherited her mother's talents and was under her guidance."

"I would have been sorry, Mr. Knightley, to have relied on your recommendation if I had left the Woodhouse family and needed a new position. I don't think you would have spoken well of me to anyone. I'm sure you always thought me unsuitable for the role I held."

"Yes," he said with a smile, "you're better suited to being a wife than a governess. But while you were at Hartfield, you were preparing yourself to be an excellent wife. You may not have given Emma the comprehensive education you were capable of, but you were learning from her about the importance of submitting to others and doing as you were told. If Weston had asked me to recommend a wife, I would have suggested Miss Taylor."

"Thank you," she said. "It won't be difficult to make a good wife to someone like Mr. Weston."

"Why, to be honest, I'm afraid you're being underutilized, and with every inclination to be patient, there may be nothing to tolerate. We won't give up hope, though. Weston may become irritable due to the comforts of life, or his son may cause him trouble."

"I hope not that," she said. "It's unlikely. No, Mr. Knightley, don't predict problems from that quarter."

"Not I, indeed. I'm just mentioning possibilities. I don't claim to have Emma's talent for predicting and guessing. I hope, with all my heart, that the young man will have the merits of a Weston and the fortune of a Churchill. But Harriet Smith – I've only just begun to discuss Harriet Smith. I think she's the worst possible companion for Emma."
}

  "passage_id": "AUSTEN_EMMA_003",
  "condition": "paraphrase",
  "rewritten_text": "You don't need to be told to express sorrow for his disappointment, I suppose. 

\"You think I should refuse him, then,\" said Harriet, looking down. 

\"Refuse him? My dear Harriet, what are you implying? Are you uncertain about how to respond? I thought I understood your intentions, but perhaps I was mistaken. I had assumed you were seeking my advice only on how to phrase your answer.\"

Harriet remained silent. With a hint of reserve, Emma continued, \"I gather you intend to give him a favourable response.\"

\"No, I don't mean that... What should I do? Please, dear Miss Woodhouse, tell me what you think I ought to do,\" Harriet asked. 

\"I won't offer you any advice, Harriet. This is something you must decide based on your own feelings,\" Emma replied. 

\"I had no idea he felt so strongly about me,\" Harriet said, pondering the letter. Emma maintained her silence for a moment, but fearing the letter's flattery might be too persuasive, she decided to speak up. 

\"As a general rule, Harriet, if a woman is uncertain about accepting a man, she should refuse him. If she hesitates, she should say no immediately. It's not a decision to be taken lightly with mixed feelings or a half-hearted attitude. I felt it was my duty as a friend, and someone older than you, to share my thoughts. However, don't think I'm trying to influence your decision.\"

\"Oh, no, I'm sure you're too kind to... but if you could just guide me on what to do... No, I don't mean that. As you said, one's mind should be made up. One shouldn't be indecisive. It's a serious matter, after all. Perhaps it would be wiser to say no. Do you think I should say no?\" 

\"Not for anything in the world would I advise you either way,\" Emma said with a gracious smile. \"You must be the best judge of your own happiness. If you prefer Mr. Martin above all others, if you think him the most agreeable man you've met, why should you hesitate? You're blushing, Harriet. Is someone else on your mind at this moment? Harriet, don't deceive yourself; don't let gratitude and compassion cloud your judgment. Who are you thinking of right now?\"

The signs were encouraging. Instead of responding, Harriet turned away, confused, and stood by the fire, lost in thought. Although she still held the letter, she now twisted it idly in her hand. Emma waited anxiously for Harriet's decision, but with strong hopes. At last, with some hesitation, Harriet said, 

\"Miss Woodhouse, since you won't give me your opinion, I must do the best I can on my own. I've now made up my mind, almost... to refuse Mr."
}
